claim: MWAA sold 424 acres of Dulles Western Lands to Digital Realty for $236.5M in Sept 2018, netting ~$207M earmarked to reduce airline rentals, fees, and charges (CPE).
source_title: Airport Land Sale Expected to Help Lower Dulles Ticket Prices
supporting_excerpt: After transaction costs, just over $200 million will be put into a special fund dedicated to controlling Dulles International's cost per enplaned passenger in future years... net an estimated $207 million... earmark the money to reduce the costs it includes when calculating rentals, fees and charges it assesses.
caveat: Prior Western Lands sale was a different parcel than the currently proposed data center inside RWY 19R/1L surfaces; precedent shows mechanism and grant-assurance treatment, not identical siting.

claim: Dulles Western Lands were acquired 2005-2007 to build a fourth runway; only the surplus was sold after the runway and support area were built.
source_title: The Airports Authority Announces Sale of 424 Acres of Western Lands at Dulles International
supporting_excerpt: The Western Lands are part of an 854-acre tract acquired by the Airports Authority between 2005 and 2007 to construct a fourth runway and additional facilities. After building the runway and support area, the Western Lands portion of the property has remained undeveloped.
caveat: Text as summarized from search of the MWAA release and WTOP reporting; confirm exact wording against the release before quoting verbatim.

claim: Data center operator paid $236.5M for the Dulles land; proceeds directed to controlling cost per enplaned passenger.
source_title: Data center operator to pay $237M for land near Dulles Airport
supporting_excerpt: Digital Realty acquired the 424 acre parcel in September 2018 for $236.5 million from MWAA... acquired between 2005 and 2007 to construct a fourth runway and additional facilities.

claim: FAA Grant Assurances 24/25 require a rate structure making the airport as self-sustaining as possible and that airport revenue be spent on the airport, favoring fair-market non-aeronautical development.
source_title: Airport Improvement Program Grant Assurances for Airport Sponsors (2025)
supporting_excerpt: Assurance 24 requires sponsors to set rates and charges to make the airport as self-sustaining as possible; Assurance 25 requires airport revenues be expended for airport-related purposes.
caveat: Excerpt paraphrased from search summary of the FAA assurances page; verify exact assurance text before quoting.

claim: FAA compliance guidance treats non-aeronautical development as legitimate at fair market value; below-FMV non-aeronautical leases are the revenue-diversion risk, not development itself.
source_title: FAA Order 5190.6C, Airport Compliance Manual Chapter 12
supporting_excerpt: Sponsors are required to charge fair market value to non-aeronautical tenants; below-fair-market-value non-aeronautical leases are treated as a form of revenue diversion.
caveat: Summarized from search; confirm chapter/section reference in the primary order.

claim: FAA publishes a Thermal Exhaust Plume Impact on Airport Operations technical guidance and assessment tool to evaluate plume effects, i.e., it is an assessable question with a defined method.
source_title: Technical Guidance Assessment Tool: Thermal Exhaust Plume Impact on Airport Operations
supporting_excerpt: The FAA has developed a Thermal Exhaust Plume Impact on Airport Operations: Technical Guidance and Assessment Tool to evaluate the effects of thermal plumes on airport operations.
caveat: Direct WebFetch of the PDF returned HTTP 403; existence and title confirmed via FAA-hosted search result. Retrieve the PDF for exact threshold text before final publication.

claim: The 4.3 m/s (~850 fpm) vertical velocity is the critical screening threshold for thermal plume hazard; exceedance triggers site-specific meteorological analysis, not automatic denial.
source_title: Thermal Plume Analysis (CEC filing referencing plume velocity threshold)
supporting_excerpt: Plume velocities in excess of 4.3 m/s is considered a potential hazard to aircraft operations... a more rigorous analysis including site-specific meteorology should be used if screening thresholds are exceeded.
caveat: Source is a CEC filing citing the threshold's aviation lineage; the '4.3 m/s' figure is widely used but the original basis is noted as uncertain. Prefer the FAA plume tool as the authoritative citation.

claim: FAA has a formal policy for reviewing solar projects on federally obligated airports, using the Sandia Solar Glare Hazard Analysis Tool; approval requires demonstrating no glare in the tower cab and no/low after-image on approach.
source_title: FAA Policy: Review of Solar Energy System Projects on Federally-Obligated Airports (2021)
supporting_excerpt: the sponsor must demonstrate that the proposed solar energy system has no potential for glint or glare in the existing or planned Airport Traffic Control Tower cab, and no potential for glare or low potential for after-image along the final approach path.
caveat: Analog for data-center lighting mitigation, not a data-center-specific rule; demonstrates FAA has a mature test-and-condition regime for light hazards.

claim: Form 7460-1 aeronautical study is the designed FAA vehicle to evaluate surface penetration, NAVAID interference, EMI, and to attach conditions to near-airport structures.
source_title: FAA 7460 Approval - Proposed Buildings, Structures, Cranes, etc.
supporting_excerpt: Circularization in the aeronautical study process occurs after the sponsor files FAA Form 7460-1 when it is shown the structure would exceed obstruction standards, require a change in an aeronautical operation or procedure or have an effect on an airport or VFR air traffic.
caveat: Secondary consultant source; the primary is FAA Order JO 7400.2 and 14 CFR Part 77. Use for process framing only.

claim: Ashburn/Loudoun is the densest data center market in the world, carrying an estimated 70% of global internet traffic, with Dulles directly behind it.
source_title: Data Center Alley: Ashburn, VA's Data Center Hub (2026 Guide)
supporting_excerpt: It is the densest data center market in the world, and an estimated 70% of global internet traffic passes through it... Dulles International Airport behind it.
caveat: Widely cited industry estimate; precise measurement of 'global internet traffic' share is imprecise.

claim: Data centers generate ~30% of Loudoun County annual tax revenue (~$586M) and return roughly $13 per dollar spent.
source_title: How Virginia became the world's data center capital
supporting_excerpt: the businesses within Data Center Alley account for 30 percent of the county's annual total tax revenue - they bring in $586 million, and for every dollar spent, data centers return about $13.
caveat: County-level figure; not airport revenue. Illustrates regional value density, not MWAA's specific take.

claim: Airport data-center leasing is a national pattern with multiple named recent projects (Buckeye, Cedar Rapids, Manassas, Colorado Springs) leveraging existing airport power and fiber.
source_title: Maximizing Airport Land with Data Centers
supporting_excerpt: Buckeye Municipal Airport (2,069 acres, up to 20M sq ft, 1.8GW); Eastern Iowa Airport ($750M project, ~$1B property tax over 20 yrs); Manassas Regional (Amazon 20 acres, $27.72M, $4-6M/yr); Colorado Springs Peak Innovation Park.
caveat: Secondary aggregator; individual figures should be confirmed against primary local sources before publication.

claim: FAA frames exhaust plume turbulence as occurring only in a limited area above the stacks, supporting the view that impacts are localized and mitigable.
source_title: FAA Finally Issues Guidance on Plume Hazards to Aircraft from Power Plants
supporting_excerpt: Exhaust plumes can create hazards for aircraft by turbulence caused by the plume's upward motion and reduced oxygen inside the plume, but only in a limited area above the stacks.
caveat: Secondary legal commentary; use to characterize plume localization, not as primary FAA text.
